groundTruthNarrative: Cedar Hollow's teller turnover rise is real (reconciled to payroll) and exceeds the in-state peer rise (28% to 47% vs 33% to 38%), so the regional labor market is at most a partial explanation. The supplied evidence cannot yet say what drives the excess. Pay, the March 2026 two-Saturday requirement, the April 2026 ShiftWise rollout at the 19 highest-volume branches, and branch-manager quality all remain live; the data that would separate them (separations by branch and corrected manager, turnover by rollout status before and after April, and a current pay benchmark) exist or can be bought but were never assembled. Exit-survey evidence is thin (19% self-selected response; manager option new in 2026) and pay was cited at the same rate the year before. A 15% across-the-board raise costs $2.6M a year, is irreversible, and could be targeted in January once a benchmark exists. Disciplining managers named from impressions and a stale manager-of-record field would punish managers who inherited their branches mid-year and who at ShiftWise branches do not control schedules. The right step is to gather the three discriminating pieces of evidence before committing.

answers.rationale: Not supported: the exit survey has a 19% self-selected response, and pay was cited at nearly the same rate before the rise (58% in FY2025 vs 61% in FY2026, E4), so the pay citations do not track the increase; the only market data are six postings chosen because candidates mentioned them, including a licensed universal-banker role and part-time retail (E6); and the last benchmark is from May 2023, when pay sat at the 51st percentile (E5). Not contradicted: pay rose only 2.5-3% a year since 2023, offer acceptance fell and 9 of 14 declines cite higher pay (E7), and the bank's market position today is unmeasured (E5), so pay erosion could still be the main driver. Rival drivers (Saturday policy, ShiftWise, managers) are equally unresolved. The COO's claim that 'nothing else changed' (E1) is false (E8, E9), but that does not settle pay either way. Monthly separations rose before any internal change (Oct-Feb FY2026 avg 11.0 vs 7.2 a year earlier, E3), consistent with pay/market pressure, but stepped up again from March when schedule changes hit, so neither pay nor its rivals is shown to be primary.

No breakdown of turnover by branch, region or manager exists (E2); the Regional VP's list rests on complaints and branch visits (E12), and the manager-of-record field is stale (E13). The 36% of exit respondents citing their manager (E4) cannot be compared with the prior year because the option did not exist then, and does not show concentration in a few branches. Nothing shows the rise is spread evenly either, so the claim is live but neither supported nor contradicted.

Tempting because schedule complaints jumped (19% to 48%, E4) and a ShiftWise teller describes 7-day posting as a problem (E10). But separations had already risen before any internal change (Oct-Feb avg 11.0 vs 7.2, E3) and stepped up again in March, before the 13 April go-live, coinciding both with the all-branch Saturday requirement (E9) and with the bank-wide announcement of ShiftWise on 4 March (E8); exit respondents and schedule-citers come from ShiftWise branches in proportion to their 52% headcount share (16 of 31; 8 of 15, E4, E8), but the sample is small and self-selected; and the pilot branches were chosen as the highest-volume branches (E8), a confound. The absence of a further firm-wide step in April cannot exclude a branch-level effect at 52% of tellers. No turnover rates by rollout status exist, so the claim can be neither supported nor ruled out.

Peer median turnover rose 5 points (33% to 38%) in the same tightening market (E14), while Cedar Hollow's reconciled turnover rose 19 points (27.9% to 46.8%, E2), and Cedar Hollow went from below the peer median to well above it. Whatever share the labor market explains, it does not explain the whole excess.

Both years' counts reconcile to payroll final-pay records (115 and 193) and both exclude transfers and promotions (E2). The rise also shows in independent records: VAC-COVER overtime and time-to-fill (E15, E7). The migration did not inflate the count.

The edge is branch-level: does deploying ShiftWise at a branch raise that branch's turnover? There are no turnover figures by branch or rollout status (E2). The only branch-tagged data, exit respondents, come from ShiftWise branches in proportion to their headcount share (E4, E8), so they do not even show an association. Firm-wide timing cannot isolate ShiftWise because separations were already rising from October and stepped up in March under the all-branch Saturday policy and the bank-wide ShiftWise announcement (E3, E8, E9). One teller's account (E10) is a single anecdote. The evidence is insufficient to say the two are associated.

Unemployment fell from 4.4% to 3.5%, peer turnover rose, and Cedar Hollow's offer acceptance fell with declines citing competing offers (E14, E7). The labor market and turnover move together. But Cedar Hollow's internal changes (Saturday policy, ShiftWise) happened over the same period and no comparison isolates the market effect, so causation is not established.

They co-occur. Monthly voluntary separations stepped up from about 11 to 16 in March 2026, the month the two-Saturday rule took effect (E3, E9). Schedule citations in the exit survey rose from 19% to 48% (E4), and both a teller and a manager link departures to the extra Saturday (E10, E11). But the survey sample is small and self-selected, ShiftWise was announced to all tellers at all branches on 4 March, the same week the Saturday rule took effect, so anticipation of ShiftWise is a live rival for both the March step and schedule complaints at non-ShiftWise branches (E8), and a spring rise also appeared in FY2025 (E3). No rival is ruled out, so it is not causal; the co-occurrence rules out 'unknown'.

No measure of manager performance is linked to any turnover figure: no branch or manager breakdown (E2), a stale manager field (E13), and a manager option in the exit survey with no prior-year comparison (E4). The Regional VP's assertion (E12) is not data. The evidence cannot show even an association.

VAC-COVER overtime can be recorded only against a system-validated open requisition, so the mechanism is in the record itself. Those hours rose from 2,140 to 9,760 and tracked open requisitions month by month, while other teller overtime was flat (E15). Longer time-to-fill extends the vacancies (E7). Mechanism, covariation and a flat comparison series establish the link.

It would be right if below-market pay were confirmed as the main driver, but that is unestablished (I1): there has been no benchmark since 2023 (E5), the posting scan is anecdotal (E6), and the survey is thin (E4). The raise costs $2.6M a year and cannot practically be reversed, and a targeted adjustment can still go in through the January 2027 cycle if approved by 2027-01-05 (E16). Waiting for a benchmark therefore does not cost the year the COO fears (E1). It is not harmful: there is no evidence it would worsen outcomes; it may simply be mis-targeted.

The PeopleCore manager field is stale for the seven branches that changed managers (E13), so using it for bonus withholding would charge FY2026 turnover to the wrong managers. Three of the five named branches got new managers between May and July 2026 (E13). At ShiftWise branches, including Harbor Point, managers cannot set schedules (E8), and the Saturday rule was imposed bank-wide (E9). The list itself rests on impressions (E12). The plan would punish parties who are partly or wholly not responsible, not merely act too early.

The breakdown directly tests H2/R4 (managers) and H3/R1 (ShiftWise, with a pre/post comparison that addresses the high-volume selection confound). It uses accurate branch cost-center data and takes about 10 business days (E13), so it arrives well before the budget lock and the vendor notice deadline. It is among the best next actions.

The pay hypothesis cannot be tested without a current market position (E5); the data is purchasable (E5, E14). It also lets any pay response be sized and targeted through the January 2027 cycle (E16) rather than set at an arbitrary 15%.

Holding the expansion is free with 30 days' notice (E8) and avoids widening a possible cause, so it is reasonable. It is not among the best actions: it does not resolve any hypothesis, and the branch/rollout analysis (about 10 business days, by 2026-12-01, E13) can be finished before the 30-day notice deadline (2026-12-12) for the 2027-01-11 go-live, so the hold is not yet needed. It is not harmful or premature, because it is reversible and commits to no diagnosis.

The rise is real and exceeds peers (E2, E14), but every candidate internal driver (pay, Saturday policy, ShiftWise, managers) remains undiscriminated. There is no current benchmark (E5) and no branch, manager or rollout-status breakdown (E2, E13), and the exit survey is a 19% self-selected sample with a changed instrument (E4). The missing data is cheap and quick, and the January cycle preserves the option to act on pay (E16).
